cards.title: 3.1 Describing Rational Functions
body: 3.1 Describing Rational Functions

**Definition:** A **Rational Function** is a real-valued function of the form $$f(x) = \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}$$, where $$P(x)$$ and $$Q(x)$$ are polynomial functions, and the denominator $$Q(x)$$ is not the zero polynomial (i.e., $$Q(x) \neq 0$$).

### Deep Dive
Rational functions extend our understanding of polynomial functions in the same way that rational numbers extend our understanding of integers. Just as a rational number is the ratio of two integers, a rational function is the ratio of two polynomials. This mathematical structure introduces new behaviors that are not possible with simple polynomials, such as discontinuities and asymptotic paths. These features make rational functions highly versatile for modeling complex real-world situations.

cards.title: Rational Functions
body: In physics and chemistry, rational functions are used to model inverse relationships, such as Boyle's Law. Boyle's Law states that the pressure $$P$$ of a gas is inversely proportional to its volume $$V$$ when temperature is kept constant ($$P = \frac{k}{V}$$). Similarly, in medical science, rational functions can model the concentration of a medication in a patient's bloodstream over time, helping doctors design safe and effective dosing schedules.

The most distinctive feature of rational graphs is their **asymptotes**. An asymptote is a line that the graph of a function approaches arbitrarily closely as $$x$$ or $$y$$ grows without bound. Rational functions can have three types of asymptotes: vertical, horizontal, and oblique (slant) asymptotes. Each type of asymptote represents a specific mathematical limit of the rational relationship.

body: is mathematically undefined, a rational function is not defined for any value of $$x$$ that makes the denominator polynomial $$Q(x)$$ equal to zero. Therefore, finding the domain of a rational function requires solving the equation $$Q(x) = 0$$. The domain then consists of all real numbers except these calculated roots, written in interval notation as a union of open intervals.

In contrast to polynomials, which have a domain of $$(-\infty, \infty)$$, the graphs of rational functions are often broken into separate branches by these domain restrictions. For example, the parent rational function, known as the reciprocal function $$f(x) = \frac{1}{x}$$, is undefined at $$x = 0$$. Its graph consists of two distinct curves that occupy the first and third quadrants of the coordinate plane, separated by the y-axis.

cards.title: Rational Functions
body: Determining the range of a rational function algebraically can be more challenging than finding its domain. One reliable method for finding the range of a one-to-one rational function is to find its inverse function, $$f^{-1}(x)$$, by swapping the variables $$x$$ and $$y$$ and solving for $$y$$. The domain of this inverse function is mathematically equal to the range of the original function, showcasing the deep connections between these algebraic structures.

cards.title: Rational Functions
body: **Vertical Asymptotes** occur at values of $$x$$ that cause the denominator to equal zero, provided those factors do not cancel with the numerator. If a factor $$(x - c)$$ in the denominator does cancel with a factor in the numerator, it produces a **point of discontinuity** (or "hole") at $$x = c$$ instead of an asymptote. This distinction is crucial: a vertical asymptote represents an infinite split where the function's values head toward positive or negative infinity, while a hole is simply a single missing point on an otherwise continuous curve.

cards.title: Rational Functions
body: Rational functions are widely used in economics and business to model **average cost structures**. While the total cost of producing $$x$$ units of a product can be modeled by a polynomial function $$C(x)$$, the average cost per unit is given by the rational function $$\overline{C}(x) = \frac{C(x)}{x}$$. Analyzing this average cost function helps businesses identify the optimal production level that minimizes per-unit costs, preventing inefficiencies.

| Expression Category | Mathematical Example | Is it a Rational Function? | Primary Reason |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Polynomial** | $$f(x) = x^3 - 2x^2 + 5$$ | Yes | Can be written as $$\frac{x^3 - 2x^2 + 5}{1}$$ |
| **Rational** | $$f(x) = \frac{3x - 5}{x^2 - 4}$$ | Yes | Ratio of two valid polynomials with $$x^2 - 4 \neq 0$$ |
| **Non-Rational (Radical)** | $$f(x) = \frac{\sqrt{x} + 2}{x - 1}$$ | No | The numerator contains a radical, which is not a polynomial |
| **Non-Rational (Exponential)**| $$f(x) = \frac{e^x}{x^2 + 1}$$ | No | The numerator is an exponential function, not a polynomial |

> **💡 Did You Know?**: The graph of the reciprocal function $$f(x) = \frac{1}{x}$$ forms a plane curve called a rectangular hyperbola, which was first studied by the ancient Greek mathematician Menaechmus in the 4th century BCE.

cards.title: 3.2 Graphing Rational Functions
body: 3.2 Graphing Rational Functions

**Definition:** **Graphing Rational Functions** involves analyzing the geometric properties of $$f(x) = \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}$$, specifically finding its intercepts, symmetry (even or odd), vertical/horizontal/oblique asymptotes, and points of discontinuity.

### Deep Dive
Graphing a rational function transforms complex algebraic equations into a visual landscape. Unlike polynomial graphs, which are smooth and continuous curves, rational graphs are often split into separate branches. To sketch these graphs accurately, we must identify their key landmarks. One of the first landmarks to look for is **symmetry**. A rational function is **even** if $$f(-x) = f(x)$$, meaning its graph is symmetric across the y-axis. It is **odd** if $$f(-x) = -f(x)$$, meaning its graph is symmetric across the origin. Identifying this symmetry early simplifies graphing, as one

cards.title: Rational Functions
body: **Horizontal Asymptotes** describe the behavior of the function as $$x$$ approaches positive or negative infinity. To find the horizontal asymptote of $$f(x) = \frac{a_m x^m + \dots}{b_n x^n + \dots}$$, we compare the degrees of the numerator ($$m$$) and denominator ($$n$$). If $$m < n$$, the line $$y = 0$$ is the horizontal asymptote. If $$m = n$$, the horizontal asymptote is the ratio of the leading coefficients, $$y = \frac{a_m}{b_n}$$. If $$m > n$$, the graph does not have a horizontal asymptote, but it may have an oblique asymptote.
